newsitem.title: INDIA: Gold - Subcontinent prospects seen mixed.
newsitem.headline: Gold - Subcontinent prospects seen mixed.

text.p: Gold prices are seen mixed in the sub-continent this week, with wedding season demand pushing up prices in India while the appreciation of the Pakistani rupee against the dollar will weaken prices there, traders said.
Indian traders said wedding season demand for gold would stem last week's fall in gold prices and local prices would be largely determined by world price trends.
The price of 24 carat gold fell 15 rupees to 4,795 rupees per 10 gramme while 22 carat fell 15 rupees to 4,435 rupees per 10 grammes.
Prices of gold biscuits (116.50 gramme each) fell by 100 rupees to 56,100 rupees per piece during the week to Monday.
"Actually, early during the week gold was distinctly weak on the back of sharp losses in the world market," said Babubhai Jain, a leading Bombay dealer.
"Arrivals of gold through unofficial channels remained low in the second half of January due to strigent vigilance by police ahead of Republic Day but now arrivals have picked up again," he added.
"Actually fluctuations in the local market are likely to remain dependent on the trend in the world market," Jain said.
"Looking at the physical inquiries for wedding season, I am expecting any fall in the prices to be short-lived in the local market," he added.
Dubai traders said low bullion prices at the end of the Islamic holy month of Ramadan combined with India's wedding season have buoyed wholesale and retail demand for gold.

Dubai's benchmark Ten Tola bar -- 3.746 ounces of 24-carat gold -- was quoted by traders at 4,772 UAE dirhams ($1,300) on Sunday, off the week's low of 4,630 but still below the 4,880 dirhams quoted in late January.
TT bars were quoted at 5,055 dirhams at the beginning of 1997 but have tracked lower world prices since the fourth quarter.
"Import demand into Dubai is phenomenal. It's not just the time of year, but the prices," one trader said. "People ran into the market and bought anything they could."

The Eid al-Fitr holiday, which marks Ramadan's end and began on February 8, also helped boost demand. The holiday traditionally involves the exchange of gifts, often in the form of jewellery or bullion.

"The import demand into India is also going very well. Ramadan is over, the wedding ceremonies are taking place, people have been paid for their crops and they are investing their money in gold and silver," he said.

Traders said the demand into India was also boosted by the Indian government's decision in December to allow non-resident Indians (NRIs) to import 10 kg of gold every six months at a customs duty of 220 rupees ($6.13) per 10 grams (0.35 oz). They were previously only allowed to import five kg.
Market participants said they expected the surge in demand to continue as long as gold prices stayed below $350 an ounce.
"But if the price stabilises around $340-$345, the excitement will start wearing off and the demand will start dipping," a trader said.
In Pakistan's commercial centre of Karachi, gold prices would fall in the next few days as the Pakistani rupee strengthened against the dollar in the kerb market, dealers said on Monday.
The strong rupee, which closed at 40.90 to the dollar on Sunday, up from 41.30 last Tuesday, depressed gold prices last week, but silver prices were unchanged, one dealer said.
GOLD PRICES 24 CARATS PER 10 GRAMMES IN U.S. DOLLARS
(Conversion $=35.90 Indian rupees 40.22 Pakistani rupees and 3.67 UAE Dirhams)
* Bombay prices February 17/10, Karachi February 16/09 and Dubai Feb 16.
